# A knowledge base with enola

A team that keeps decisions beside its code (a wiki, ADRs, a design log)
can compile them into the graph. Then a file answers which decision
governs it, a decision answers which code it covers, a structural claim
in prose can be re-checked mechanically, and a finding judged once stays
judged. This guide is that practice, as it runs day to day on a
twenty-repository knowledge base.

> This guide builds the practice by hand, small enough to read and run
> without any tool of its own. [tabula](13-tabula.md) is the same practice
> as one program: its pages, contract, laws compiled into
> `enola/constraints/`, receipts and gates. The table at the end of that
> guide says which piece here each of its verbs replaces.

## Pages compile into the graph

A markdown page carrying an `enola_intent:` block is an intent fact when
the snapshot is taken, and every anchor on it is an edge to a file:

```yaml
---
title: Charges run through one service
enola_intent:
  page:
    type: decision
    status: accepted
    scope:
      - shop
    relations:
      - rel: supersedes
        to: wiki/adrs/charges-in-controllers.md
    anchors:
      - repo: shop
        path: app/billing/charge.rb
      - repo: shop
        path: app/billing/refund.rb
---
```

Derive the block rather than hand-maintain it: if your pages already cite
the code they describe (`sources:` lines naming repository paths), the
anchors are those citations, and a small script stamps the block from
them and checks the derivation in CI. enola validates the block; keeping
it truthful to your conventions is yours.

Index the knowledge base as a member of the cluster, last, so its pages
compile over the code they anchor:

```yaml
repos:
  - ../shop
  - ../mobile
  - .
```

## Ask the graph what governs a file

```bash
enola plan -paths app/billing/charge.rb .
```

and over MCP, `governing_intent` for a file or a symbol: the pages whose
anchors cover it, with their relation trails (what supersedes what, what
depends on what), and for a page, which code its anchors cover. A file no
page governs is an answer too, and the difference between "no page
governs this" and "the graph was not asked" must stay visible: a missing
snapshot is a named skip, never silence.

This is the call behind the [intent-first gate](10-hooks.md): before an
agent's first edit into a repository, the governing pages are read.

## Laws over the pages

Because anchors are facts, laws can read them (see [writing
laws](04-writing-laws.md)):

```ruby
part :billing, files: "app/billing/**"
part :old_way, governed_by: "wiki/adrs/*.md status:superseded"
part :new_way, governed_by: "wiki/adrs/charges-in-one-service.md"

law "billing is documented" do
  billing.must_be_governed
  why "code under a decision needs the page that decided it"
end

law "the new way never reaches the old" do
  new_way.must_not_call :old_way
  why "a superseded decision's code is on its way out, not a dependency"
end
```

## Receipts are the committed state

Graph artifacts (`.enola/`, the cluster's output directory) are
machine-local and ignored. What enters version control is the receipt:
one entry per repository with the snapshot's fingerprint, the commit it
was taken at, the enola version and the providers that ran. Keep them in
one file the knowledge base owns:

```json
{"repos": {"shop": {"fingerprint": "…", "git_commit": "…", "enola_version": "0.4.34", "providers": ["prism", "rubydex"]}}}
```

Two rules follow. **Regenerate the whole cluster, never one member**: a
snapshot scoped to one repository replaces the union rather than
updating its slice, and everything that reads the union then answers
from a narrower world without saying so. **Not comparable is not a
pass**: when a member's snapshot changed enola version or provider set,
the grade declines; re-pin and regenerate rather than reading silence as
clean.

## Citations with a grammar

A structural claim in prose ("`internal/facts` has 157 dependents")
cites the receipt it was read from, in one fixed shape, so a script can
re-check it against the committed receipts and flag the ones whose
digest moved. The shape is yours to choose; what matters is that there
is one, that one extractor parses it, and that a periodic sweep lists
every citation with a verdict (verified, stale, malformed). A claim
nobody can re-check is a sentence, not a fact.

## Findings are judged once

The explainers report candidates, not verdicts: a cycle at 0.7
confidence, a god class, an unused route. Before a finding grounds a
page, confirm it against the code and record the judgment in a ledger
beside the receipts, one entry per finding signature: accepted (and
where it landed), rejected, or permanent noise. The next session reads
the ledger instead of re-deciding, and the periodic sweep reports a
ledger entry whose finding no longer exists, which is the code moving
past a recorded judgment.

## Pulled, with one push

Skills fetch the graph while already reasoning about something: a
deepdive asks `impact_analysis` and `governing_intent`, an ingest checks
a claim with `query_facts` while the source is open, a drift sweep
regenerates and diffs receipts. Nothing lands on a board because the
graph said so. The one exception is the session-end hook, which speaks
only when the session's change introduced a structural regression, or
when it could not grade at all; a gate nobody remembers to run is no gate.

## The wrapper

Every skill calls a thin command the knowledge base owns rather than
the binary: `kb enola generate | receipt | diff | findings | judge | impact
| govern | citations | baseline | check | coverage | doctor`. It resolves
the binary, the cluster config and the receipts file, and when any is
absent it prints one line saying so and exits 0. That is what keeps a
skill from failing on a machine without enola, and what keeps "the graph
was not asked" distinguishable from "the graph agreed". The [wrapper
guide](12-the-wrapper.md) has its shape.

# Hooks: the graph at the moments that matter

A hook fires at a moment nobody has to remember: a session starting, the
first edit into a repository, a turn ending, a push. Each one here reads
the graph at that moment, blocks at most once, and forces a reading,
never a verdict. The scripts are in [`templates/hooks/`](../templates/hooks);
they are written for Claude Code's hook protocol (JSON on stdin, exit 2
to block with the message on stderr) and translate to any agent with
hooks.

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md), `tabula install --harness claude` writes the
> gate, the record, the debt and the session hooks this guide wires by hand,
> and `--uninstall` removes exactly what it wrote. The hand-wired scripts
> below are the same ideas, short enough to read.

## enola's own pair

```bash
enola install --hooks
```

wires two: **session start** pins the architecture as the session's
baseline; **stop** grades what the session changed against it and speaks
only when the change introduced a regression or could not be compared. In
Claude Code it adds a third, a `PreToolUse` hook that refuses the
session's first two file searches until an enola tool is used; it sits
beside the intent-first gate below without overlapping it. `enola doctor` reports when each last fired and what it
concluded; a hook that never fires is the failure to look for.

## The intent-first gate (PreToolUse on Edit and Write)

The first write into each repository per piece of work is blocked once.
The block carries two things: the pages that govern the file
(`governing_intent`, or `enola plan -paths <file>` when the MCP is not
in reach) and the pre-edit contract (the declared laws binding the path
and the blast radius over the current snapshot). The agent reads, then
retries, and the retry proceeds. The gate re-arms on every user message,
so each ask gets its own forced stop and no piece of work gets two.

What it refuses to do: decide. If the governing page contradicts the
intended change, the contract says amend the page first; the hook only
makes the page impossible to miss. When no page governs the file, it
says so and asks whether the work should be shaped. When the graph is
absent, it says so and lets the write through; a missing graph is a
named skip, never a wall.

`templates/hooks/intent-first-gate.sh` gates Edit and Write. The brain's
own gate also classifies shell commands as writes (a `sed -i`, a
redirect, a `cp` into the repository); the template marks where that
classifier goes and leaves it out, because the rules for what counts as a
write depend on your tree.

## The stop-time debt (Stop)

When the turn ends, two debts can block it once each:

- **Code moved, no spec moved.** Files changed in a governed repository
  this turn and no governing page did. The block asks for either the
  amendment or an explicit sentence, in the reply, saying why the pages
  as written already cover the change.
- **A push went out with no grade.** A `git push` to a repository
  happened this turn and no `enola check` ran. The block asks for the
  grade, read, before finishing.

Both read a small per-session record the PostToolUse hook writes
(`templates/hooks/record.sh`): which files moved, whether a push
happened, whether a check ran. The debt hook is the mechanical half of
two rules a team can otherwise only ask people to remember.

## The union refresh (SessionStart)

When the session starts, compare the paired repository's HEAD with the
commit the committed receipt records. When they differ, regenerate that
member's slice of the union in the background and say so in one line;
when they agree, say that. The agent's first structural question then
reads a graph that matches the checkout it is about to edit.

## Wiring

Claude Code, in `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{"matcher": "startup|resume", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "enola hook session-start"},
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/hooks/session-refresh.sh\""}]}],
    "PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/hooks/intent-first-gate.sh\""}]}],
    "PostToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/hooks/record.sh\""}]}],
    "UserPromptSubmit": [{"hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/hooks/record.sh\" reset"}]}],
    "Stop": [{"hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "enola hook stop"},
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/hooks/stop-debt.sh\""}]}]
  }
}
```

## What it feels like

An agent asked to change a billing service edits nothing until it has
read the decision that put charges through one service; it grades the
change before the push and writes the grade into the pull request; and
when it ends the turn having changed code under a decision without
touching the decision, it is asked to account for that once. None of
this needs the agent to know enola exists.

# The skills, as they run

A skill is a named piece of practice an agent follows. Each of these asks
the graph one specific question at one specific moment; the value is the
moment, not the prompt. They are described here as they run on a
twenty-repository knowledge base, and shipped under
[`templates/skills/`](../templates/skills) to copy.

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md), one `tabula` skill and the loop it runs
> (search, claim, govern, align, impact, baseline, grade, report, release)
> take the place of the five skills below; they stay here as the practice
> written out.

## Before shaping work: the deepdive (`enola-deepdive`)

Shaping a change starts with three graph questions, answered before a
line of the plan is written:

- `impact_analysis` on every symbol the work would change: fan-in,
  fan-out, named callers. A symbol with 157 dependents is a different
  plan from one with 3.
- `governing_intent` on the paths: which decisions already cover the
  area, so the plan amends a page rather than contradicting it.
- `query_insights` for the area: what the explainers already computed (a
  cycle someone must have introduced, a layer crossed, a dead route), so
  the plan inherits judged findings instead of rediscovering them.

The plan cites the receipt it read from, so a later reader can re-check
the numbers.

## Before building: the grade (`enola-grade-before-push`)

`set_baseline` once, early; after the change, `generate_snapshot` and
`diff_snapshot`; the delta (introduced, resolved, edges added) goes into
the pull request in one sentence. A declined comparison is not a pass.
This is also the [stop-time debt](10-hooks.md) hook's demand.

## While ingesting a source: the claim check (`enola-ingest-check`)

A page that states a structural fact (a stack, a public surface, a
route, a table) checks it while the source is open: `query_facts` for
the fact, `impact_analysis` for the count. A wrong claim ingested today
is cited by a page tomorrow and reasoned from by an agent next week, so
verification is cheapest now. For an incremental ingest, each changed
path runs through `governing_intent`: the pages whose anchors cover a
changed file are exactly the synthesis that may have drifted, and a
changed file no page governs is a gap the ingest may be about to fill.

## The periodic sweep: drift (`enola-drift`)

On a schedule, or before publishing: regenerate the cluster, diff the
committed receipts (fingerprint and commit per member), and read
`coverage_report` for which cross-repository edges resolved and which did
not. Receipts that moved name the members whose pages want a re-read.
Not a comparison of findings between two runs; that is the grade's job.

## Knowledge hygiene: citations and the ledger (`enola-citation-hygiene`)

Every receipt citation in prose gets a verdict against the committed
receipts: verified, stale (the digest moved), malformed. Stale ones are
re-read, not rewritten. The finding ledger is swept the same way: an
accepted finding whose evidence no longer exists in the graph is the
code moving past a judgment, and the page that cites it is re-read.

## Stepping back: the blast radius (`enola-zoom-out`)

When deep in a change, one call answers how it sits in the whole:
`impact_analysis` for the symbols in hand, `find_path` between the
part being changed and the parts that consume it, `governing_intent`
for the decisions around it. The answer is one paragraph of technical
fit the agent can stand on, beside the product fit it reasons out.

## Writing and explaining laws (`enola-laws`)

Covered in [writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): lint before verdict,
`constraints explain` before arguing with a verdict, ratchet before
strict.

## What makes these skills and not prompts

Each names the call, the moment, and the refusal: what the agent does
when the graph is absent (say so, proceed, never pretend), when the
comparison declines (re-pin, never read as clean), when a finding is a
candidate (confirm against the code, judge once, record). That is the
practice the hooks enforce and the skills describe; the two are one
contract read from two sides.

# The wrapper

Skills call a command the knowledge base owns, not the binary. The
wrapper is thin: it knows where the binary, the cluster config and the
receipts file live, it records receipts after a generate, and when
anything is absent it prints one line saying so and exits 0. That is the
whole design, and it is what lets every skill run on a machine without
enola without failing, while keeping "the graph was not asked" a
different sentence from "the graph agreed".

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md) there is no wrapper to write: `govern`,
> `impact` and `evaluate` ask the engine themselves and say "not asked"
> rather than pass, which is the named skip this guide builds.

## The operations

| Op | Answers |
|---|---|
| `generate` | snapshot the cluster, then record every member's receipt |
| `receipt [member]` | what was recorded |
| `diff` | which members' live receipts drifted from the recorded ones |
| `findings [--repo] [--all]` | the explainers' findings across the cluster, attributed to the member their evidence names, with judged ones hidden |
| `judge <signature> accepted\|rejected\|noise` | record a verdict in the ledger |
| `impact <symbol>` | fan-in, fan-out, named callers, read from the on-disk facts |
| `govern <path or page>` | the pages governing a file, or the code a page anchors |
| `citations` | every receipt citation in prose with its verdict |
| `baseline pin\|show\|clear [member]` | the "before" a change is graded against |
| `check [member]` | the grade, reported, never gating |
| `coverage` | which cross-repository edges resolved |
| `doctor` | whether the hooks fire |

## The shape, in any language

```
resolve binary   -> absent: print "enola: not installed, the graph was not asked"; exit 0
resolve config   -> absent: print the path looked for; exit 0
resolve receipts -> absent on a read op: print; exit 0
run the op       -> on generate, read each member's .enola/receipt.json
                    and write fingerprint, commit, version, providers
                    into the receipts file
exit codes       -> the binary's, except check: report, exit 0
```

Three things to keep:

- **Receipts are the only committed state.** `generate` writes them;
  nothing else does. `diff` compares them to the live ones; it is not a
  comparison of findings.
- **Findings read from disk, not the MCP server.** `impact` and
  `findings` parse the fact and insight files, so scheduled and headless
  runs keep working when no server is up.
- **`check` reports; it never gates.** The binary exits 1 on a
  regression and the wrapper does not propagate it: no graph-dependent
  step may stop work, so the verdict is surfaced for a person to weigh.
  Exit 3 from the binary means the snapshots were not comparable; the
  wrapper prints that as "not asked", never as a pass.

## The ledger beside the receipts

```json
{"findings": {"cycles|app/jobs -> app/models -> app/jobs": {"verdict": "accepted", "at": "2026-08-22", "reason": "real; the mailer path", "landed": "wiki/shop/permanent/architecture.md"}}}
```

One entry per finding signature, written on judgment. There is no
pending state: nothing enumerates unjudged findings as work, because a
finding nobody bet on is an observation.

## Why not call the binary directly

Every skill would then carry the absent-binary branch, the config
resolution and the receipt bookkeeping, and they would drift. The
wrapper is where those live once, which is why the guides say `kb enola
impact` where the brain that runs this says `brain.py enola impact`.

# tabula: the knowledge base, kept by a tool

Guides 09 to 12 build a knowledge base by hand: pages anchored to code, a
wrapper, four hooks, five skills, receipts and a ledger. [tabula](https://github.com/misabegovic/tabula)
is that practice as one program. It keeps the pages, checks them against
a contract, compiles their laws into enola constraints, grades a plan
against the code with enola, and holds every agent that works on the
code to the page that governs it. This guide is what an enola user needs
to know to start; tabula's own documentation under `docs/wiki/` goes
further, and every verb prints the command to run next and why.

## What it adds to enola

enola measures what the code is and grades what a change did to it.
tabula holds what the code should be, in pages a person writes:

- **Architecture pages** (`.tabula`, `kind: architecture`) draw parts and
  arrows and state laws as sentences; `tabula architecture --write`
  compiles them into `enola/constraints/` in the repository, so the
  repository's own `enola check` enforces them with no tabula in CI.
- **PRDs** (`kind: initiative`) carry acceptance bullets, each settled by
  an observation: a test to run, a count over the facts, or
  `grade: enola check clean`. `tabula evaluate` settles every bullet as
  met, not met, not checked or does not apply, with no model involved,
  and writes the verdict into the decision record beside the PRD with a
  receipt.
- **The loop**: search before reading, claim before working, find the
  governing page before editing, grade before finishing, report what
  happened. Hooks refuse an edit until the agent has recorded the page it
  is working from.

## Install

A tabula release carries cardo, the build of enola it is developed
against, inside the binary. Download the archive for your platform from
the [releases](https://github.com/misabegovic/tabula/releases), check it
against `SHA256SUMS`, and put `tabula` on your PATH:

```bash
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf tabula-0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz
install -m 755 tabula-0.0.1-linux-amd64/tabula ~/.local/bin/tabula
tabula doctor
```

v0.0.1 is built for linux-amd64 only. On any other platform, build from a
clone with `cargo build --release` (the repository pins its Rust
toolchain); a plain build carries no engine and uses the one on your PATH.

The carried cardo is unpacked into tabula's cache the first time a verb
needs it, its digest checked, and it is **found last**: `engine.binary` in
`tabula.config.yml` comes first, then `cardo`, `cardo-current` and `enola`
on your PATH. An upstream `enola` you installed for the other guides is
therefore the engine tabula runs, with a warning on every line that
carries its result. `tabula doctor` says which engine answered and how it
was found (`engine` and `carried` lines); set `engine.binary` to choose
one, or `engine.carried: never` to leave the carried copy out. tabula
never installs or upgrades an engine of its own accord.

## The first run

```bash
mkdir shop-brain && cd shop-brain
tabula init --tour
tabula tour
```

`init --tour` writes an empty project (a `wiki/`, an `AGENTS.md` stating
the contract, `tabula.config.yml`) and a small inherited shop with the
facts an engine already read from it, so the tour runs without one.
`tabula tour` names the one command to run next, read off the project
each time: write a page, find it with `search`, `explain` the shop from
its facts, `picture` its architecture page, then `evaluate` a PRD the
shop does not meet yet, fix one line, and evaluate it again.

For your own code, name the repositories in `tabula.config.yml`
(`projects_root`, `active_repos`) and let the engine draft a first page:

```bash
tabula explain shop --generate
```

writes a page a newcomer can read, every sentence a claim with its file
and line, and, when the repository has no architecture page yet, a draft
at `wiki/shop/architecture/explained.tabula` that forbids nothing.

## Laws, from a page to `enola check`

```bash
tabula say shop/architecture/shop.tabula "orders never calls gateway." \
  --because "billing alone talks to the payment gateway."
tabula architecture shop/architecture/shop.tabula --write
```

`say` writes the law under the page's `***laws***` and reads it back with
what the code shows today, a count and never a verdict. `--write` puts
the compiled rules in the repository:

```yaml
# enola/constraints/shop.yaml
# Compiled by `tabula architecture` from the page `shop/architecture/shop.tabula`; edit the page, not this file.
components:
  - name: orders
    match: ["shop/orders.py"]
  - name: gateway
    match: ["shop/gateway.py"]
rules:
  # orders never calls gateway.
  - id: orders-never-calls-gateway
    forbid: orders
    to: gateway
    via: calls
    mode: ratchet
    since: 2026-10-25
    because: >-
      billing alone talks to the payment gateway.
```

That file is plain enola YAML, and upstream enola v0.4.34 lints it clean.
Commit it in the repository and grade it there exactly as
[constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md) describes. A sentence with no
strength word is `ratchet`; `, as a warning.` is `advisory` and
`, without exception.` is `strict`. A rule no sentence can say is written
in enola's own form under `laws/` at the project root, and `tabula
export` copies it into the repository with the compiled pages.

## A plan graded against the code

```text
***specs***

- An order's total counts every line, discounts included.

  ***acceptance***

  - A discount line lowers the total.
    test: ~/projects/shop/tests/test_totals.py -- python3 -B -m unittest tests.test_totals
  - The change crosses no law.
    grade: enola check clean
```

`tabula evaluate shop/prds/totals-add-up.tabula` runs the test and asks the
engine for `check --json --fail-on=constraints` on every repository the
PRD anchors. A regression, whole or partial, is not met; no baseline,
incomparable snapshots or no engine is "not checked", never a pass. A
bullet not met exits 5, and the fix is in the code: tabula's rule is that
the bullet, its observation and the checked block are never edited to
make a verdict pass.

## Agents

```bash
tabula install --harness claude      # or agents, pi, codex
```

opens tabula's doors to one harness: for Claude Code, hooks in
`.claude/settings.json`, a `tabula` MCP server in `.mcp.json` and a
skill, each file recorded in `wiki/_state/install.json` so `--uninstall`
removes exactly what it wrote. The `agents` harness covers anything that
reads `AGENTS.md` (opencode, goose, Cline, OpenHands, Amp). tabula's
repository is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace, under
`editors/claude-code`, carrying the same server, hooks and skill plus the
`.tabula` language server.

The skill's rule is one line: search before reading, claim before
working, evaluate before finishing. The loop it runs is
`tabula run loop --flow`: search, claim, find the governing page with
`govern`, record it with `align` (or write the intent first), check the
blast radius with `impact`, pin a baseline, edit from the aligned
bullets, grade, report, release. The edit gate refuses a write until
`align` has recorded the page the change is generated from, and a write
from the shell is caught by git's status, not by reading the command.

tabula's hooks and enola's (`enola install --hooks`) do different jobs
and sit side by side in `.claude/settings.json`: enola's pin a baseline,
grade the session and turn the first searches toward the graph; tabula's
hold the agent to the page. Install enola's first. In v0.4.34, running
`enola install --hooks` again after tabula's are in place adds enola's
stop hook a second time, inside tabula's stop entry, so the session is
graded twice per turn; if you re-run it, remove the copy.

## Which hand-built piece tabula replaces

| Guides 09 to 12 | With tabula |
|---|---|
| a script stamping `enola_intent:` onto a page | intent lives under `intent:` on the page; `tabula export` writes the frontmatter mirror the engine's `mdintent` extractor reads |
| laws in the Ruby DSL beside the page | `***laws***` sentences on the architecture page, compiled by `tabula architecture --write` (the Ruby DSL still works beside them) |
| a receipts file and a citation sweep | receipts under `wiki/_state/receipts/`, re-checked by `tabula verify`; `tabula check` for citations, links and scope |
| a findings ledger | the inbox, where only a person confirms or dismisses a finding, beside `enola constraints ledger` |
| the wrapper (`kb enola …`) and its named skip | the verbs themselves: `govern`, `impact`, `evaluate`, each saying "not asked" rather than passing |
| the intent-first gate | `tabula hook gate`, which refuses until `align` records the governing page |
| stop-time debt | a stop hook that blocks until the change is aligned or reverted |
| hand-wired hook settings | `tabula install --harness claude`, or the plugin |
| the five knowledge-base skills | the one `tabula` skill and the loop's govern, impact, baseline and grade steps |

The hand-built path stays documented because it is what tabula does,
written small enough to read and run without it.

## Next

- tabula's [tutorials and how-tos](https://github.com/misabegovic/tabula/tree/main/docs/wiki):
  explain your own repository, add a constraint to a repository, run
  tabula in CI, connect a harness over MCP.
- [taha](14-taha.md): agents that run on a tabula project under a
  mandate, stopping to ask before anything is published.

# taha: agents under a mandate

[taha](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha), short for tabula harness, is a
command-line tool that runs coding agents on a [tabula](13-tabula.md)
project and keeps them on track. You say what you want; taha routes it
through tabula's intent pages (a pitch, a plan, a decision record, then
the build), runs the agent, settles routine questions with a council of
reviewers, and stops to ask you before anything is published. taha
decides nothing tabula can decide: every gate it applies is a tabula
verdict, and a bug in taha can at worst stop a run, never let a failed
check through.

This guide is where taha meets enola. taha's own
[first hour](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha/blob/main/docs/first-hour.md)
fixes one bug in a sample project in ten stops with no model and no
account, and [the menu](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha/blob/main/docs/menu.md)
lists every command by goal; start there.

## Install

taha is not on npm yet, and the name `taha` on npm belongs to another
package, so `npm install -g taha` installs something else. Install from a
clone, with Node 22.19 or newer, on Linux or macOS (Windows through WSL):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/misabegovic/taha && cd taha
npm install
npm link
taha help
```

taha runs the tabula `TABULA_BIN` names, else the newer of the tabula its
platform package carries and the one on your PATH. A clone has no platform
package, so [install tabula](13-tabula.md#install) first.

## What a run is

One piece of work, an issue or a PRD slug, is one durable conversation
kept in SQLite under `state/`, so a crash or a restart never repeats an
act. The run claims the piece with `tabula claim`, attaches `tabula serve`
over the project, and journals every committed step into the project's
journal. Before a piece can finish `done` or open a pull request,
`tabula evaluate` must read every acceptance bullet met; a PRD bullet
written as `grade: enola check clean` is how enola's verdict becomes one
of them.

What the run may do is written in a mandate, `wiki/mandates/default.md`:
the acts it may take (`allow`, `ask`, `never`), its budget, whether it is
`supervised` or `autonomous`, the repositories in scope, the test command,
and when it expires. GitHub is reached through one connector whose only
writes are a branch, a push, a draft pull request and a comment; each is
journaled before it runs, a pull request is always a draft, and taha has
no way to mark one ready or merge it. Anything public waits in the inbox
for you:

```bash
taha                       # what runs, what waits on you, what is next
taha approve <finding>     # a yes to what waits
taha steer <run> <words>   # change a run in flight
taha stop <run>            # stop at the next safe point
```

## Adopting a repository that enola already measures

```bash
cd ~/src/shop
taha adopt --inside        # or --beside --repo shop, to write nothing into it
taha doctor
```

`adopt --inside` adds the project's files to the repository, records the
repository's own checks so a push waits for them, and, for the code map,
writes `mcp-arch.yaml` and runs `cardo --generate` in the repository.
`adopt --beside` writes nothing into the repository and leaves the
snapshot to you. `taha doctor` prints one line each for the layout, the
mandate, the state folder, the schedule and the code map, and exits 0
when all of them read `ready`.

taha calls the engine as `cardo`, by that name on your PATH; it does not
fall back to `enola`. The cardo a [tabula release](13-tabula.md#install)
carries is unpacked into tabula's cache, and `tabula doctor` prints where
(the `engine` line). Until cardo has an install of its own, link that copy
onto your PATH for taha:

```bash
ln -s "$HOME/.cache/tabula/engine/<digest>/cardo" ~/.local/bin/cardo
```

An `mcp-arch.yaml` the repository already has is left as it is, so the
providers [guide 02](02-rails.md#the-two-providers) configures keep
running.

## Where enola's laws stay

taha adds no law of its own. The laws are the repository's
`enola/constraints/`, written by hand or compiled from tabula's
architecture pages, and they are graded by the repository's CI with
`enola check` as [guide 05](05-constraints-in-ci.md) describes, whoever
or whatever wrote the change. taha's part is to make an agent's run reach
that CI only as a draft, after tabula's checks, with you asked first.

# A Python service

What enola measures in a Python codebase, the laws a Python team states,
and the one place the shipped recipes need a hand. The worked example is
[`examples/python-service`](../examples/python-service): a FastAPI
service in four packages that breaks three laws on purpose, snapshotted
by CI on every change to this repository.

## Install

```bash
pip install enola-cli        # the PyPI name; the command is enola
enola --version
```

`enola` was taken on PyPI, so the project is `enola-cli`; it is the same
binary as the install script and the GitHub release. `pipx install
enola-cli` or `uv tool install enola-cli` keeps it out of your project's
environment. Then the loop from [start here](01-start-here.md):

```bash
enola --explain .
enola --generate .
enola baseline pin .
```

## What enola measures

A tree is Python when it carries `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`,
`requirements.txt`, `Pipfile` or one of the tool configs, at the root or
up to three levels down. Parsed with tree-sitter, never imported:

- **Modules are directories.** `shop/api` and `shop/domain` are modules;
  a law's `match:` globs select files, and the module edges between
  directories are what cycles and layers read.
- **Imports** are `imports` edges, each tagged `internal`, `external` or
  `stdlib`. Calls are `calls` edges from a function to what it calls,
  with the calls made inside a loop recorded on the caller for N+1
  hunting.
- **Routes** from FastAPI and Flask, at their composed runtime path:
  `include_router(r, prefix="/p")` folds `/p` onto every route `r`
  declares, across files.
- **Storage** from SQLAlchemy models, each with its table name.
- **Module-level code** (what runs at import time) is kept on a
  `file_ref`, an edge carrier rather than architecture.
- **Tests** (`tests/`, `test_*.py`, `conftest.py`) are reference-only.

What it leaves out on purpose: a route whose path is not a literal, a
mount with a computed prefix (its routes keep their bare paths), routes a
plugin registers at import time, and dispatch through `getattr`.

## The laws

The `layered` recipe names four roles. Bind them to your packages:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["shop/api/**"] }
      application: { match: ["shop/services/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["shop/domain/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["shop/repositories/**"] }
```

Its three rules over `calls` hold on Python as written: the API reaches
the services only, services never call back into the API, repositories
never drive the services. In the example, a route that reads a
repository directly breaks the first one:

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: shop/api/orders.list_recent -> shop/repositories/orders.recent_orders via calls
```

**Its two domain rules read `depends_on`, and Python's extractor writes
`imports`,** so on a Python tree they are silent whatever the domain
imports. `via:` names one edge kind exactly. State the domain's law over
the edge Python has:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["shop/domain/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["shop/repositories/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain that imports a table cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: module-edge: shop/domain -> shop/repositories -> shop/repositories via imports
```

`ports-and-adapters`, `clean` and `modular-monolith` are the other
arrangements enola ships; read which `via:` each rule names before
binding one, and run `enola constraints lint .` after a snapshot to see
what every part resolved to.

## Dependencies

Each direct dependency in `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt` is a
fact (`pkg:pypi/fastapi`), pinned when the constraint is `==` or a
lockfile resolves it. The `supply-chain` recipe is the law that every one
is pinned:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: supply-chain
    as: supply
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      unpinned-dependencies: {}
```

```text
Constraint supply/dependencies-are-pinned violated: pkg:pypi/fastapi is measured in supply/unpinned-dependencies
```

## Explainers worth gating on

- **`import-closure`** answers what `import shop` actually executes,
  including the `__init__.py` files no import names, and names the
  initialisations responsible for most of it: a barrel written for
  convenience that makes importing the public API load a scraping
  library. The barrels it names are gateable with
  `-fail-on import-closure`.
- **`query-loops`** reports a call that reaches storage inside a loop
  over input, the N+1 candidates.
- **`cycles`** between packages, which Python allows and an import at
  function scope hides from a reader.

For CI, [constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md) and enola-action
apply unchanged; the Rubydex step is for Ruby and can be dropped.

# A TypeScript or JavaScript service

What enola measures in a TypeScript or JavaScript codebase, the laws a
Node team states, and the two places the code's shape decides what a law
can see. The worked example is
[`examples/typescript-service`](../examples/typescript-service): an
Express service in four directories that breaks three laws on purpose,
snapshotted by CI on every change to this repository. Front ends have a
guide of their own for Ember ([guide 03](03-ember.md)); Angular, Vue,
Nuxt, Svelte and Next.js are read by the same extractor.

## Install

enola is not on npm. Install the binary once per machine:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

or `pip install enola-cli`, or a binary from the
[releases](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases) for Linux, macOS
and Windows. Then the loop from [start here](01-start-here.md).

## What enola measures

- **Modules are directories**; `import … from` is an `imports` edge,
  tagged `internal` or `external`, and a call is a `calls` edge from the
  function that makes it.
- **Server routes** from Express (mounts composed across files), NestJS
  (controller prefixes composed), InversifyJS, and file-based routing in
  Next.js, Nuxt and SvelteKit.
- **Client calls** (`fetch`, axios, Angular's `HttpClient`, a wrapper
  another file exports) as client routes, which the cluster linker
  matches to a server's routes ([guide 08](08-beyond-one-repo.md)); an
  in-house client is declared under `clients:`.
- **Storage** from Prisma, TypeORM and Drizzle, each with its physical
  table name; a Drizzle query flags the function doing I/O.
- **GraphQL** operations and schema-first servers, **Kafka** and AsyncAPI
  contracts.

## The laws

Bind the `layered` recipe to your directories:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["src/routes/**"] }
      application: { match: ["src/services/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["src/domain/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["src/db/**"] }
```

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: src/routes.listRecent -> src/db.recentOrders via calls
```

**A handler's calls belong to the handler only when it has a name.** An
inline arrow, `router.get("/recent", async (req, res) => …)`, puts its
calls on the file's `file_ref`, which the edge rules do not walk, so the
same breach written inline reports nothing. Name the handler (an
exported function the router registers) and the route also carries a
`handled_by` edge to it, which is what `enola endpoint` and the
route-scoped laws follow.

**The recipe's two domain rules read `depends_on`, and the TypeScript
extractor writes `imports`,** so they are silent on a TypeScript tree.
State the domain's law over imports:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["src/domain/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["src/db/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain that imports a schema cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: src/domain -> src/db/schema -> src/db/schema via imports
```

In v0.4.34 an Express `router.post("/", …)` mounted at `/orders`
produces no route, while `router.post("/create", …)` comes out as
`POST /orders/create`; a law or a coverage count over a router's root
path does not see it yet.

## Dependencies

Each direct dependency in `package.json` is a fact (`pkg:npm/express`),
pinned when its constraint is one exact version or `package-lock.json` or
`yarn.lock` resolves it. A `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `bun.lockb` beside the
manifest leaves `pinned` absent, since enola cannot read it, and a law
over `pinned` then says nothing rather than something false. The example
has no lockfile, so its `^4.19.2` is a breach of `supply-chain`:

```text
Constraint supply/dependencies-are-pinned violated: pkg:npm/express is measured in supply/unpinned-dependencies
```

## A provider of your own

eslint's findings join the graph through the reference provider in
enola's `examples/providers/js/eslint/`, a Node script under two hundred
lines that reads the results file your lint step writes; configure it as
[providers](07-providers.md) shows.

# A Go service

What enola measures in a Go codebase, and the laws worth writing where
the compiler already forbids an import cycle. The worked example is
[`examples/go-service`](../examples/go-service): a chi service in four
packages that breaks two laws on purpose, snapshotted by CI on every
change to this repository.

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

enola is written in Go, and a source build is `go install ./cmd/enola`
from a clone of [enola-labs/enola](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola),
with Go 1.26 or newer and a C compiler for the tree-sitter bindings. The
prebuilt binary needs neither. Then the loop from
[start here](01-start-here.md).

## What enola measures

- **Packages are modules**, imports are `imports` edges between them, and
  calls are `calls` edges from the function that makes them, including a
  function used as a value (a dispatch-table entry, a callback).
- **Routes** from `net/http`, gin, chi and the other routers, with prefixes
  composed across function boundaries; outbound HTTP calls as client
  routes; gRPC and Kafka on both sides.
- **Loops**: a call made inside a loop over input is recorded on the
  caller, which is what `query-loops` reads for N+1 candidates.
- **Multi-module repositories**: imports resolve through every `go.mod`
  in the repository, so a monorepo with one module per service, or a
  module nested in another, gets internal edges between them rather than
  external, unresolved ones.

## The laws

Go's compiler refuses an import cycle between packages, so gating on
`cycles` enforces what the toolchain enforces first. The laws a Go team
needs are the ones no compiler states: which package may reach which.

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["internal/web/**"] }
      application: { match: ["internal/checkout/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["internal/order/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["internal/store/**"] }
```

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: internal/web.listRecent -> internal/store.RecentOrders via calls
```

**The recipe's two domain rules read `depends_on`, and Go's extractor
writes `imports`,** so they are silent on a Go tree. State the domain's
law over imports:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["internal/order/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["internal/store/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain package that imports the store cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: internal/order -> example.com/shop/internal/store -> internal/store via imports
```

Go's own `internal/` rule stops another module importing your internals;
a `forbid` between two of your own `internal/` packages is the rule it
leaves to you.

## Dependencies

A `require` in `go.mod` names an exact version, so every direct
dependency is pinned and `supply-chain` holds; the example binds it and
it reports that its part matches nothing. `// indirect` lines are the
closure and are not read.

# A Rust service

What enola measures in a Rust crate, the laws a Rust team states, and two
places where v0.4.34 reads less than the code says. The worked example is
[`examples/rust-service`](../examples/rust-service): an Axum service in
four modules that breaks two laws on purpose, snapshotted by CI on every
change to this repository.

## Install

enola is not on crates.io. Install the binary once per machine:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

or `pip install enola-cli`, or a binary from the
[releases](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases). Then the loop
from [start here](01-start-here.md).

## What enola measures

- **Crate and module directories are modules**; `use crate::store::…` is
  an `imports` edge, a call is a `calls` edge, a constructor call an
  `instantiates` edge, and a method in an `impl` a symbol with its
  receiver.
- **Routes** from Axum, `.nest("/p", other::router())` folded onto every
  route the nested router declares across files, and from
  `#[utoipa::path]` attributes, one route per declared verb.
- **Complexity and loops** per function.

## The laws

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["src/web/**"] }
      application: { match: ["src/checkout/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["src/order/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["src/store/**"] }
```

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: src/web.list_recent -> src/store.recent_orders via calls
```

**The recipe's two domain rules read `depends_on`, and Rust's extractor
writes `imports`,** so they are silent on a Rust crate. State the
domain's law over the `use` edge:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["src/order/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["src/store/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain module that uses the store cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: src/order -> crate::store::latest_total -> src/store via imports
```

## Where v0.4.34 reads less

- **A nested router built inline keeps its bare paths.**
  `.nest("/orders", Router::new().route("/recent", …))` records
  `GET /recent`, while the same router returned from a function,
  `.nest("/orders", orders())`, records `GET /orders/recent`. The example
  uses the function form.
- **A Cargo version with no operator counts as pinned.** `axum = "0.7"` is
  a caret range in Cargo, but without a `Cargo.lock` enola marks it
  `pinned: true`, so `supply-chain` does not report it; `"^0.7"`, `"~0.7"`
  and `">=0.7"` are read as ranges. Commit `Cargo.lock` for a binary
  crate, which pins every dependency whatever its constraint says. The
  example keeps the bare `"0.7"`, and its `EXPECTED` file records that
  the law is silent, so CI notices the day enola reads it.
files.recipes/README.md:
# Recipes

A recipe is a named bundle of architecture laws over roles. A repository
binds it in its `enola/constraints/` declaration and the laws apply to the
code the roles select. The recipes here are starting points: copy one into
your repository's `enola/recipes/`, read every `because:`, change what your
team decides differently, and review it like any other file. A convention
nobody on the team wrote is not a convention.

## Binding a recipe

Roles carry selector defaults (`match`, `kind`, `name_pattern`, `where`), so
a binding is the recipe's name and the mode:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: ember-conventions
    as: app
    mode: ratchet
```

Override a role's selector when your tree differs, key by key:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: ember-conventions
    as: app
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      components: { match: ["frontend/app/components/**"] }
```

A role marked `optional: true` carries no default because its selector is
yours to name: the law that references it expands away until you bind it.
`enola constraints lint` lists the rules left unexpanded for that reason.

Modes: `ratchet` reports what already breaks the law and fails only what a
change adds; `advisory` reports and never fails; `strict` fails on every
breach. Start with ratchet.

## The recipes

The catalogue munola ships built in: `munola init` writes these recipes
into a project's `enola/recipes/` and binds those whose roles resolve,
and the munola binary embeds the parameter-free ones, generated from
these files at release. The `enola` and `enola-rb` gems carry upstream's
own built-ins only (`rails-conventions`, `rails-strict`, `vanilla-rails`,
`ruby-conventions`, `supply-chain` and the six arrangements); a team on
those channels copies a file from here by hand. Each law is
an existing enola form; each recipe is here because its laws held on a real
Rails monolith at a number a team can act on, given beside it.

| Recipe | States | Held at |
|---|---|---|
| `rails-conventions` (upstream) | jobs, models, serializers and components never render; policies and mailers never enqueue; request API stays in controllers | five of seven laws with zero exceptions, three advisory at 134 crossings |
| `rails-strict` (upstream) | the above plus no cycles among the Rails roles and independent concerns | 0 of 127 concerns breach |
| `vanilla-rails` (upstream) | the directories the vanilla arrangement leaves empty stay empty | an arrangement a team chooses |
| `ember-conventions.yaml` | nine Ember conventions selected by what the code carries | the neutral eight hold; the house ones stay out |
| `data-ownership.yaml` | readers read the store only | advisory; bind your query objects |
| `api-boundaries.yaml` | the public API is reached only by controllers; a mutating action reaches a policy | 736 unauthorized mutations reported, advisory |
| `background-work.yaml` | maintenance tasks live in their namespace and never reach controllers | 0 of 3,250 task call edges reach a controller |
| `tenant-foreign-key.yaml` | a table carrying the tenant column carries the foreign key | 3,720 declared, 0 new |

Two data-ownership laws, one owner per table and storage stays home, are
declarations rather than recipe rules for now: they live as worked examples
under [`examples/laws/`](../examples/laws/README.md) because recipe expansion
in the current release does not rebind the part a graph law names. They join
`data-ownership.yaml` when it does.

- `ember-conventions.yaml`: nine Ember conventions a team can adopt as laws,
  selected by what the code carries (a decorator, a written field, a base
  class's module) rather than by where it sits. Two optional roles are
  yours to bind: `task-factories` (the functions that make tracked tasks or
  tracked functions in your app) and `fixture-setup` (the entry points of
  your fixture library in tests).

- `data-ownership.yaml`: readers (your query objects, bound by you) reach
  the store and nothing else.
- `api-boundaries.yaml`: the API layer is entered through controllers, and a
  mutating action reaches a policy; bind `mutating-actions` to the part your
  routes reach with POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
- `background-work.yaml`: maintenance tasks live in the `Maintenance`
  namespace the runner resolves, and never reach controllers.
- `tenant-foreign-key.yaml`: a template; replace `TENANT_COLUMN` and
  `TENANT_TABLE` (munola's generator does) and every table carrying the
  column must carry the key.

Laws whose far end is a helper of your own (a promise-unwrapping getter
helper, an async-relationship reader) belong in your repository's recipe
beside these, with your names in them.

recipe: api-boundaries
roles:
  - name: controllers
    match: ["app/controllers/**"]
  - name: policies
    match: ["app/policies/**"]
  - name: public-api
    match: ["app/controllers/api/**"]
  - name: mutating-actions
    optional: true
rules:
  - id: public-api-reached-only-by-controllers
    protect: public-api
    owners: [controllers]
    via: calls
    mode: advisory
    because: "The API layer is entered through a request so that authentication, rate limits and serialization run once, at the edge; an internal caller that reaches an API class directly skips all three and nobody reading the API can see it."

  - id: mutations-are-authorized
    require_edge: mutating-actions
    to: policies
    direction: outbound
    via: calls
    mode: advisory
    because: "Every write passes a policy before it touches a record. Bind the actions that routes reach with POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE (a part declared with handles: on those methods) and the law names each mutating action that reaches no policy."

recipe: ember-conventions
roles:
  - name: components
    match: ["app/components/**"]
  - name: integration-tests
    kind: test_ref
    match: ["tests/integration/**"]
  - name: actions
    kind: symbol
    where: { decorators: action }
  - name: framework-controllers
    kind: symbol
    where: { superclass_module: "@ember/controller" }
  - name: constructors
    match: ["app/**"]
    name_pattern: "*.constructor"
  - name: fetchers
    match: ["app/services/**"]
  - name: legacy-accessor
    match: ["app/utils/**"]
    name_pattern: "*.get"
  - name: argument-mutators
    kind: symbol
    where: { fields_written: args }
  - name: element-modifiers
    kind: symbol
    match: ["app/components/**", "app/modifiers/**"]
  - name: state-writing-members
    kind: symbol
    where: { fields_written: "<any>" }
  - name: task-factories
    optional: true
  - name: fixture-setup
    optional: true
rules:
  - id: no-action-decorator
    forbid_fact: actions
    because: "An arrow function binds lexically and needs no decorator; the decorator predates it and the convention says to stop writing it."

  - id: no-framework-controllers
    forbid_fact: framework-controllers
    because: "A route component replaces the controller and its template. Controllers are quirky and carry surprising singleton state, and the convention is to stop adding them."

  - id: components-import-no-render-modifiers
    forbid: components
    to_name: ["@ember/render-modifiers*", "ember-render-helpers*"]
    via: imports
    because: "The render-helper form fires on a lifecycle rather than attaching to the element it acts on, and it has been discouraged for years. A named modifier attaches to the element and says what it acts on."

  - id: constructors-do-not-fetch
    forbid: constructors
    to: fetchers
    via: calls
    because: "Rendering pulls data in as it is needed. A constructor that fetches is eager, runs before anything asks, and cannot be re-run when the arguments change."

  - id: no-legacy-property-accessor
    forbid: components
    to: legacy-accessor
    via: calls
    because: "The proxy accessor reads through a layer that no longer exists on a resolved value, and it defeats type checking. Reach for the property."

  - id: arguments-are-not-mutated
    forbid_fact: argument-mutators
    because: "Data flows down and actions flow up. A component that writes through its own arguments changes state it does not own, and the owner never learns of it. Pass a callback and let the owner make the change."

  - id: a-modifier-takes-its-element
    require: element-modifiers
    when_edge_to: ["*.modifier"]
    via: calls
    must_prop_contain: { prop: takes_parameters, value: "yes" }
    because: "A modifier is handed the element it is attached to. One that declares no parameter is not modifying anything; it is a side effect fired by render, and a getter or a tracked task says that honestly."

  - id: derivations-do-not-write
    forbid: state-writing-members
    to: task-factories
    via: calls
    because: "A task is derived state and runs inside the render cycle. Writing the component's own state from one schedules another render off the render it is running in. Return the data and read it through the task's value instead."

  - id: component-tests-carry-no-fixtures
    forbid: integration-tests
    to: fixture-setup
    via: calls
    because: "A fixture library sets up back-end state and has no place in a component test: if the component makes no request, build a front-end record, and if it does, let the acceptance layer answer it."

#!/bin/bash
# Grades this pull request's architectural delta against its base branch and
# reports what the change added: declared constraints, queries in loops, layer
# violations, dependency cycles. By default findings are reported, never
# blocking (-warn-only). ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE=1 makes this a gate: the step
# then exits with enola check's own code, 1 when the change introduced a
# finding the policy fails. Turning it on is a team decision.
#
# What fails at all is enola's policy, unchanged here: a new finding from a
# watched explainer at confidence 1.00, and a strict law's breach whether new
# or not. An advisory law reports at 0.90 and never fails; neither does a
# finding an explainer only estimates (an inferred layer, a query reached
# through an interface). ENOLA_CHECK_MIN_CONFIDENCE lowers that floor, and
# advisory laws then fail with the rest.
#
# Requirements: the full history of the base branch and the change (on
# GitHub `fetch-depth: 0`, on GitLab `GIT_DEPTH: 0`), a clean working tree,
# curl, tar and sha256sum. Optional: ruby, to render the findings grouped by
# rule (without it the comment is enola's own `check --summary`), and gh,
# to post the comment (without it the comment is printed).
#
# On CI (CI set) anything that keeps the delta from being graded fails the
# step, so the check cannot go quiet; on a laptop it skips with the reason.
# The one skip on CI is a build with nothing to grade: this commit is the
# base itself.
#
# Three seams are yours to fill, marked FILL IN below: how the pinned binary
# is fetched, how the pull request's base branch is read on a push build,
# and how the comment is posted. Everything between them runs the same on
# any CI and on a laptop.
set -euo pipefail

# The enola release this check runs: ENOLA_VERSION, else the first line of a
# committed .enola-version, so a repository pins it in one place.
ENOLA_VERSION="${ENOLA_VERSION:-$(head -n 1 .enola-version 2>/dev/null || true)}"
ENOLA_VERSION="${ENOLA_VERSION:-0.4.35}"
WATCHED_EXPLAINERS="${ENOLA_CHECK_WATCHED:-constraints,query-loops,layers,cycles}"
WATCHED_FLAGS=(-fail-on "$WATCHED_EXPLAINERS")
[ -z "${ENOLA_CHECK_MIN_CONFIDENCE:-}" ] || WATCHED_FLAGS+=(-min-confidence "$ENOLA_CHECK_MIN_CONFIDENCE")
[ "${ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE:-0}" = 1 ] || WATCHED_FLAGS+=(-warn-only)

say() { echo "enola check: $1"; }

skip() {
  say "skipped: $1. The architectural delta was not graded this build."
  exit 0
}

# On CI a missing prerequisite fails the step so the check cannot go quiet;
# locally it skips.
notrun() {
  if [ -n "${CI:-}" ]; then
    say "did not run: $1. The architectural delta was not graded this build."
    exit 1
  fi
  skip "$1"
}

work=$(mktemp -d)
current_ref=""
cleanup() {
  if [ -n "$current_ref" ]; then
    git checkout -q "$current_ref" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi
  rm -rf "$work"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# FILL IN 1: fetch the pinned binary. Cached per version and platform so a
# laptop downloads once. Verify the checksum the release publishes.
os=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
arch=$(uname -m)
case "$arch" in x86_64 | amd64) arch=amd64 ;; arm64 | aarch64) arch=arm64 ;; *) notrun "no enola build for $arch" ;; esac
ENOLA="${HOME:-$work}/.cache/enola/${ENOLA_VERSION}/enola"
if [ ! -x "$ENOLA" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$ENOLA")"
  asset="enola-${ENOLA_VERSION}-${os}-${arch}.tar.gz"
  curl -fsSL "https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases/download/v${ENOLA_VERSION}/${asset}" -o "$work/$asset" || notrun "could not download enola ${ENOLA_VERSION}"
  curl -fsSL "https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases/download/v${ENOLA_VERSION}/${asset%.tar.gz}.sha256" -o "$work/${asset%.tar.gz}.sha256" || notrun "could not download the checksum for enola ${ENOLA_VERSION}"
  (cd "$work" && sha256sum -c "${asset%.tar.gz}.sha256" >/dev/null) || notrun "checksum mismatch for ${asset}"
  tar -xzf "$work/$asset" -C "$work"
  mv "$work/${asset%.tar.gz}" "$ENOLA"
  chmod +x "$ENOLA"
fi
say "enola ${ENOLA_VERSION} at ${ENOLA}"

# Providers the agent can run. Each absence is a named line, never silence,
# and the same providers feed both snapshots so they stay comparable. Both
# Ruby providers run inside the binary once the Rubydex library is fetched;
# no Ruby is needed. The binary pins the library, so neither entry carries an
# expected_version.
provider_entries=""
if [ -f Gemfile ]; then
  rubydex_fetch="$("$ENOLA" providers fetch rubydex 2>&1 | tail -n 1 || true)"
  if "$ENOLA" providers list 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^  rubydex  0\.'; then
    provider_entries="  - name: rubydex
  - name: prism
"
  else
    say "rubydex and prism providers not configured (${rubydex_fetch:-providers fetch printed nothing})"
  fi
fi

GENERATE_TARGET="$PWD"
if [ -n "$provider_entries" ]; then
  GENERATE_TARGET="$work/enola-generate.yaml"
  printf 'repos:\n  - %s\nproviders:\n%s' "$PWD" "$provider_entries" > "$GENERATE_TARGET"
fi

# A shallow clone has no merge-base to grade against; say how to get one
# rather than grading nothing.
[ "$(git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository 2>/dev/null)" != true ] ||
  notrun "this is a shallow clone; fetch the full history (fetch-depth: 0 on GitHub, GIT_DEPTH: 0 on GitLab)"

# FILL IN 2: the pull request's base branch. Pull-request builds usually
# carry it in an environment variable; push builds know the pull request
# number and must ask the forge. main only when there is no pull request.
base_branch="${PR_BASE_BRANCH:-}"
if [ -z "$base_branch" ] && [ -n "${PR_NUMBER:-}" ] && command -v gh >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  base_branch=$(gh pr view "$PR_NUMBER" --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName 2>/dev/null || true)
fi
base_branch="${base_branch:-main}"
git fetch origin "$base_branch" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
base_sha=$(git merge-base HEAD "origin/${base_branch}" 2>/dev/null || true)
[ -n "$base_sha" ] || notrun "no merge-base with origin/${base_branch}"
[ "$base_sha" != "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ] || skip "this commit is origin/${base_branch} itself, so there is no change to grade"

dirty=$(git status --porcelain -uno)
[ -z "$dirty" ] || notrun "working tree not clean, cannot generate the baseline in place"

head_ref=$(git symbolic-ref -q --short HEAD || git rev-parse HEAD)
current_ref="$head_ref"
git -c advice.detachedHead=false checkout -q "$base_sha" || notrun "could not check out the merge-base"
"$ENOLA" --generate "$GENERATE_TARGET" >/dev/null 2>&1 || notrun "baseline snapshot failed at ${base_sha:0:11}"
git checkout -q "$head_ref"
current_ref=""
"$ENOLA" --generate "$GENERATE_TARGET" >/dev/null 2>&1 || notrun "snapshot generation failed on this checkout"

# Exit 0 is clean and 1 a regression the policy fails: both are verdicts,
# rendered and posted. 3 is a declined comparison and 2 a gate that could
# not run: neither graded anything.
set +e
verdict=$("$ENOLA" check -baseline previous "${WATCHED_FLAGS[@]}" -json "$GENERATE_TARGET" 2>/dev/null)
check_exit=$?
set -e
case "$check_exit" in
  0 | 1) ;;
  3) notrun "enola declined to grade: the two snapshots are not comparable (enola check exited 3)" ;;
  *) notrun "enola check could not run (exited ${check_exit})" ;;
esac

if command -v ruby >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  summary=$(printf '%s' "$verdict" | ruby "$(dirname "$0")/enola-findings.rb")
  status=$(printf '%s' "$summary" | head -n 1)
  details=$(printf '%s' "$summary" | tail -n +3)
else
  # The verdict's own status reads "clean" under -warn-only whatever it
  # found, so the summary's sections decide: no "Got worse", nothing new.
  say "ruby is not on this agent; the comment is enola's own summary"
  plain=$("$ENOLA" check -baseline previous "${WATCHED_FLAGS[@]}" -format summary "$GENERATE_TARGET" 2>/dev/null || true)
  status=FINDINGS
  grep -q '^Got worse' <<<"$plain" || status=CLEAN
  details="\`\`\`
$plain
\`\`\`"
fi

if [ "$check_exit" -eq 1 ]; then
  blocking="**This blocks the merge.**"
elif [ "${ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE:-0}" = 1 ]; then
  blocking="**Nothing here fails the check.**"
else
  blocking="**Nothing is blocked** while the team gets used to the check."
fi

case "$status" in
  CLEAN)
    body="No new architectural findings against \`${base_sha:0:11}\`."
    ;;
  PARTIAL)
    body="enola check: no new findings against \`${base_sha:0:11}\` among the facts both snapshots share. **This is a partial verdict.**

$details"
    ;;
  DECLARED)
    body="enola check: this change declares rules that existing code already breaks, and introduces no new findings on the code it touched (against \`${base_sha:0:11}\`). $blocking

$details"
    ;;
  *)
    body="enola check found new architectural findings against \`${base_sha:0:11}\`. $blocking

$details"
    ;;
esac

# FILL IN 3: post one comment per pull request, edited in place. Without a
# forge credential, print it. The REST API edits a comment by its numeric
# id, so the lookup goes through the same API.
if [ -n "${PR_NUMBER:-}" ] && command -v gh >/dev/null 2>&1 && gh auth status >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  marker="<!-- enola-check -->"
  existing=$(gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/${PR_NUMBER}/comments" --paginate \
    --jq ".[] | select(.body | startswith(\"$marker\")) | .id" 2>/dev/null | head -n 1 || true)
  if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
    if gh api -X PATCH "repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/comments/$existing" -f body="$marker
$body" >/dev/null; then
      say "updated the existing enola comment"
    else
      say "could not update the enola comment $existing"
    fi
  elif [ "$status" != "CLEAN" ]; then
    gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" --body "$marker
$body" >/dev/null && say "posted a new enola comment"
  fi
else
  printf '%s\n' "$body"
fi

exit "$check_exit"

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "json"

LISTED = 10
EXAMPLES_PER_RULE = 3
RULES_LISTED = 12

def rule_of(finding)
  finding["title"][/constraint (\S+) violated/i, 1] || finding["source"] || "?"
end

def constraint?(finding)
  finding["source"] == "constraints"
end

def breach_of(finding)
  finding["title"].sub(/\A.*violated: /, "")
end

def render_flat(findings)
  findings.first(LISTED).each do |finding|
    puts "- **#{finding["source"] || "?"}** — #{finding["title"]}"
    fact = finding.dig("evidence", 0, "fact")
    puts "  `#{fact}`" if fact
  end
  puts "- _...and #{findings.size - LISTED} more_" if findings.size > LISTED
end

def render_grouped(findings, phrase)
  groups = findings.group_by { |finding| rule_of(finding) }
  ordered = groups.sort_by { |rule, breaches| [constraint?(breaches.first) ? 0 : 1, -breaches.size, rule] }
  ordered.first(RULES_LISTED).each do |rule, breaches|
    puts "- **#{rule}** — #{breaches.size} #{phrase.call(breaches.size, constraint?(breaches.first), strict?(breaches.first))}"
    breaches.first(EXAMPLES_PER_RULE).each do |finding|
      puts "  - #{breach_of(finding)}"
    end
    puts "  - _...and #{breaches.size - EXAMPLES_PER_RULE} more_" if breaches.size > EXAMPLES_PER_RULE
  end
  puts "- _...and #{ordered.size - RULES_LISTED} more rules_" if ordered.size > RULES_LISTED
end

def strict?(finding)
  finding["title"].start_with?("Strict constraint")
end

NEW_PHRASE = lambda do |count, constraint, strict = false|
  if strict
    (count == 1) ? "place breaks it; a strict law fails on every breach, new or not" : "places break it; a strict law fails on every breach, new or not"
  elsif constraint
    (count == 1) ? "new place breaks it" : "new places break it"
  else
    (count == 1) ? "new finding" : "new findings"
  end
end
EXISTING_PHRASE = ->(count, _constraint, _strict = false) { (count == 1) ? "existing place already breaks it" : "existing places already break it" }

verdict = JSON.parse($stdin.read)
policy = verdict["policy"] || {}
gated = policy["fail_explainers"] || []
floor = policy["min_confidence"] || 1.0
warn_only = policy["warn_only"]
watched = verdict["failures"] || []
# Findings that fail nothing: a watched explainer's below the confidence
# floor (an advisory law, an estimate), and every other explainer's.
below, other = (verdict["advisories"] || []).partition { |finding| gated.include?(finding["source"]) }
declared = verdict["declared"] || []

excluded = verdict.dig("intersection_grading", "excluded") || []

def render_partial(excluded)
  puts "**Partial verdict** — graded only the facts both snapshots share. A regression among these producers' facts is not reported:"
  puts
  excluded.each do |producer|
    puts "- **#{producer["name"]}** (#{producer["kind"]}), missing from the #{producer["lacked_by"]} snapshot"
  end
end

if watched.empty? && below.empty? && other.empty? && declared.empty?
  if excluded.empty?
    puts "CLEAN"
  else
    puts "PARTIAL"
    puts
    render_partial(excluded)
  end
  exit 0
end

puts((watched.empty? && below.empty? && other.empty?) ? "DECLARED" : "FINDINGS")
puts

if excluded.any?
  render_partial(excluded)
  puts
end

if watched.any?
  verdict_line = warn_only ? "They would fail the check once it enforces; nothing blocks today." : "They fail the check."
  puts "**Watched** — new findings from the explainers this check gates on (#{gated.join(", ")}), at confidence #{format("%.2f", floor)} or above. #{verdict_line}"
  puts
  render_grouped(watched, NEW_PHRASE)
end

if below.any?
  puts if watched.any?
  puts "**Below the floor** — new findings from the same explainers under confidence #{format("%.2f", floor)}: an advisory law (0.90) or a finding the explainer estimates. Reported, never failing."
  puts
  render_grouped(below, NEW_PHRASE)
end

if declared.any?
  puts if watched.any? || below.any?
  puts "**Declared** — rules this change declares, re-forms or un-exempts, reported on code the change did not touch. The baseline each rule starts from, not new findings."
  puts
  render_grouped(declared, EXISTING_PHRASE)
end

if other.any?
  puts if watched.any? || below.any? || declared.any?
  puts "**Also noticed** — outside the watched explainers."
  puts
  render_flat(other)
end

#!/bin/bash
# PreToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit: block the first write into each
# repository per piece of work, once, with the governing pages and the
# pre-edit contract on stderr. The retry proceeds; the gate forces the
# reading, never the verdict. Re-armed by record.sh on every user message.
#
# Where a shell-command classifier would go: a Bash tool call whose text
# carries a write shape (sed -i, a redirect, tee, cp or mv into the tree,
# an interpreter fed a heredoc) is a write too. What counts depends on your
# tree; gate it the same way once you have decided.
set -u
input=$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)
sid=$(jq -r '.session_id // "nosession"' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
file=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
[ -n "$file" ] || exit 0

top=$(git -C "$(dirname "$file")" rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
case "$file" in
  "$top"/.enola/*|"$top"/wiki/_views/*|"$top"/wiki/_state/*) exit 0 ;;
esac
rel="${file#"$top"/}"
repo=$(basename "$top")

state="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/intent-first-$(id -u)"
mkdir -p "$state"
ack="$state/${sid}-${repo}.ack"
[ -e "$ack" ] && exit 0
touch "$ack"

govern=""
if command -v enola >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  govern=$(cd "$top" && timeout 30 enola plan -paths "$rel" . 2>/dev/null | sed -n '/^Plan report/,$p' | head -40)
fi
[ -n "$govern" ] || govern="(enola plan unavailable: no binary or no snapshot for this checkout; named skip, consult the decision records by hand)"

cat >&2 <<EOF
intent-first gate (${repo}): first write for this piece of work.

Before ${rel} moves, read what governs it and check the intended change
against it. If the change deviates from what the governing page records,
amend the page first; if nothing governs this work, say so and ask
whether it should be shaped.

${govern}

Retrying proceeds. This gate re-arms on every user message; within one
piece of work it will not fire again for ${repo}.
EOF
exit 2

#!/bin/bash
# PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash: record what this turn did, so
# the stop-time debt hook can account for it. With "reset" as the first
# argument (UserPromptSubmit): a new user message begins a new piece of
# work, so clear the record and the gate's acknowledgements.
set -u
state="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/intent-first-$(id -u)"
mkdir -p "$state"
input=$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)
sid=$(jq -r '.session_id // "nosession"' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
turn="$state/${sid}.turn"

if [ "${1:-}" = "reset" ]; then
  rm -f "$state/${sid}"-*.ack "$turn" "$state/${sid}.debt-blocked" "$state/${sid}.push-blocked"
  exit 0
fi

record() { printf '%s\n' "$1" >> "$turn"; }

tool=$(jq -r '.tool_name // empty' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
if [ "$tool" = "Bash" ]; then
  cmd=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
  [ -n "$cmd" ] || exit 0
  printf '%s' "$cmd" | grep -qE '(^|[[:space:];&|])git[[:space:]]+push' && record "push"
  printf '%s' "$cmd" | grep -qE 'enola[[:space:]]+check' && record "check"
  exit 0
fi

file=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // .tool_response.filePath // empty' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
[ -n "$file" ] || exit 0
top=$(git -C "$(dirname "$file")" rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
rel="${file#"$top"/}"
case "$rel" in
  wiki/*.md|docs/decisions/*.md|docs/adrs/*.md) record "spec	$rel" ;;
  *) record "code	$rel" ;;
esac
exit 0

#!/bin/bash
# SessionStart: when a cluster member's HEAD moved past the commit the
# committed receipts record, regenerate the cluster in the background and
# say so in one line; when they agree, say that. The agent's first
# structural question then reads a graph that matches the checkout.
#
# RECEIPTS is the knowledge base's committed receipts file; CLUSTER the
# cluster config; MEMBER the repository to compare (default: this one).
set -u
RECEIPTS="${RECEIPTS:-wiki/_state/enola/receipts.json}"
CLUSTER="${CLUSTER:-enola-cluster.yaml}"
MEMBER="${MEMBER:-.}"
command -v enola >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "enola hooks: no binary on PATH; the graph was not asked (named skip)"; exit 0; }
[ -f "$RECEIPTS" ] || { echo "enola hooks: no receipts at $RECEIPTS; the graph was not asked (named skip)"; exit 0; }

label=$(basename "$(cd "$MEMBER" && pwd -P)")
head=$(git -C "$MEMBER" rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)
recorded=$(python3 - "$RECEIPTS" "$label" <<'PY' 2>/dev/null
import json, sys
r = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
print(((r.get("repos") or r).get(sys.argv[2]) or {}).get("git_commit") or "")
PY
)
if [ -n "$head" ] && [ "$head" != "$recorded" ]; then
  log="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/enola-refresh-$(id -u).log"
  (nohup enola --generate "$CLUSTER" > "$log" 2>&1 &)
  echo "enola hooks: $label is at ${head:0:11}, the recorded receipt at ${recorded:0:11}; regenerating the cluster in the background (log $log)."
else
  echo "enola hooks: the recorded receipt matches $label at ${head:0:11}."
fi
exit 0

#!/bin/bash
# Stop: block the end of the turn once when this turn pushed without a
# grade, and once when code moved under decision records and no record
# moved. Reads the per-session record written by record.sh.
set -u
state="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/intent-first-$(id -u)"
input=$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)
sid=$(jq -r '.session_id // "nosession"' <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null)
turn="$state/${sid}.turn"
[ -f "$turn" ] || exit 0

if grep -q '^push$' "$turn" && ! grep -q '^check$' "$turn" && [ ! -e "$state/${sid}.push-blocked" ]; then
  touch "$state/${sid}.push-blocked"
  cat >&2 <<'EOF'
push without a grade: this turn pushed and ran no enola check.

Before finishing: run `enola check <repo>` against the pinned baseline
and read the grade. A declined grade is not a pass; re-pin and grade
again. This check blocks once per turn.
EOF
  exit 2
fi

if grep -q '^code' "$turn" && ! grep -q '^spec' "$turn" && [ ! -e "$state/${sid}.debt-blocked" ]; then
  touch "$state/${sid}.debt-blocked"
  summary=$(awk -F'\t' '$1 == "code" { print "  " $2 }' "$turn" | sort -u | head -15)
  cat >&2 <<EOF
intent debt: code moved this turn, and no decision record did.

Changed without a record moving:
${summary}

Before finishing: either amend the governing record to match what was
built, or state explicitly, in your reply, why the records as written
already cover the change. This check blocks once per turn.
EOF
  exit 2
fi
exit 0

---
name: enola-citation-hygiene
description: Use during grooming; gives every receipt citation in prose a verdict against the committed receipts and sweeps the finding ledger for judgments the code has moved past
---

# enola-citation-hygiene: every citation gets a verdict

1. `kb enola citations`: each receipt citation in prose is verified, stale
   (the digest moved) or malformed.
2. Stale: re-read the cited page against the current facts and amend the
   sentence; never update the citation alone, the sentence is what may be
   wrong.
3. Malformed: fix the citation to the recorded form.
4. `kb enola findings --all`: for each accepted finding in the ledger,
   confirm its evidence still exists in the graph. Evidence gone means
   the code moved past the judgment; re-read the page that landed it and
   record the new state.
5. Rejected and noise verdicts stay; they keep the finding hidden on
   purpose.

A citation is a promise that a number was read, not remembered; this
skill keeps the promise current.
